title: Asteroid Vesta on the move
blurb: The brightest asteroid slides past the stars in ten hours.
story: Vesta is the brightest asteroid in the sky and the second-largest body in the asteroid belt; NASA's Dawn spacecraft orbited it in 2011–12. In these pictures from 16–17 July 2026 it is the dazzling object with the halo. In ten hours it moves about 6 arcminutes, a fifth of the width of the full Moon.

spectrum.hint: The measurements scatter too much to read a pattern. That happens when an object is so bright that it overloads the detector, or when it is changing while SPHEREx watches. Each point is a separate exposure, taken at a different time.

doodles.explain: A point of light that moved 364 arcseconds (59.2 SPHEREx pixels) toward the east in 9.8 hours, about 37 arcseconds per hour, while the stars stayed put. Only bodies inside our Solar System cross the sky that fast: an asteroid, or a comet if it looks fuzzy. This is (4) Vesta, a known asteroid (JPL Horizons).

source: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (collections spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3)
